title: Post-Scarcity Leads to Technological Stagnation
gist: Charles Rosenbauer argues Moore's Law is an economic phenomenon, not a physical one, and that it will stall not because transistors stop shrinking but because human imagination runs out of profitable uses for compute: photomask costs have gone $1M (28nm) to $10M (7nm) to $40M (3nm), fab campuses from a few billion to hundreds of billions, and cutting-edge competitors have collapsed to TSMC and Samsung. He treats LLMs as the only remaining consumer application with an uncapped appetite for hardware, and is openly skeptical that they alone can fund a trillion-dollar superfab, reframing 'post-scarcity' as Taiichi Ohno's 'overproduction' — capacity running far ahead of any order.

insights.claim: Consumer compute has outrun consumer demand for it: a sub-$1,000 laptop performs trillions of calculations per second while typical applications like text editing do nothing that a machine with a million times less compute could not do thirty years ago.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: If the marginal utility of consumer compute is already near zero, the demand case for perpetual node shrinks rests entirely on datacenter AI, not on a broad device refresh cycle.
insights.quote: compute is available in such great abundance that it exceeds our knowledge of how to put it all to productive use
insights.locator: The text editor in which this article

insights.claim: Wirth's law — software losing efficiency faster than hardware gains it — is the mechanism that has absorbed most of the last two decades of compute gains, with modern browsers like Google Chrome burning vast resources to display formatted text while a twenty-year-old video game rendered complex 3D lighting on a fraction of those resources.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: Software bloat, not end-user need, has been the hidden demand sink for Moore's Law; if efficiency ever becomes a priority, hardware demand falls further.
insights.quote: over time, software gets less efficient faster than hardware gets more efficient
insights.locator: For less than a thousand dollars, a modern consumer laptop

insights.claim: Gordon Moore's own warning that his law was an economic rather than a physical phenomenon remains unfalsified after six decades, which means the binding constraint on future computing is conceptual — knowing what to do with compute — not technological.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: Frames semiconductor cycles as demand-driven, so watch application-layer monetization rather than roadmap announcements as the leading indicator for fab capex.
insights.quote: the future of computing will be determined not by our ability to innovate technologically, but by our ability to conceptualize what this compute would be used for
insights.locator: This abundance is famously the product of Moore’s Law

insights.claim: Early computing's original demand driver — bureaucratic record processing — is computationally trivial and long since saturated, since a modern laptop could process facts about the entire world's population in under an hour.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: Enterprise record-keeping cannot be a growth market for compute; back-office software vendors sell workflow and habit, not processing power.
insights.quote: a modern laptop may be able to process facts about the entire world’s population in less than an hour
insights.locator: The Start of the Curve

insights.claim: Technology adoption lags technical capability by decades for institutional rather than technical reasons: public-key cryptography solved digital signatures decades ago, yet DocuSign still employs 7,000 people intermediating pen-and-paper conventions.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: Businesses monetizing legacy process friction can be durable even when technically obsolete — but they are also the first casualties if institutions ever modernize.
insights.quote: Public-key cryptography solved this problem properly decades ago; DocuSign still has 7,000 employees today.
insights.locator: Exponential growth in computation has rapidly overwhelmed

themes.theme: LLMs as the Last Uncapped Demand Sink

insights.claim: The large language model is the first consumer application in decades whose hardware appetite has no visible ceiling, with hundreds of millions of users routing questions, drafts, and small work tasks through chatbots that are absorbing search, customer service, and a growing share of clerical labor.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: LLM consumer usage is the single load-bearing justification for the entire compute buildout — its persistence is the key variable for semis exposure.
insights.quote: The large language model is the first consumer application in decades whose appetite for hardware has no visible ceiling
insights.locator: For the moment, artificial intelligence seems to have supplied the answer

insights.claim: Current LLM demand may sustain the AI industry at roughly its present scale once the infrastructure buildout completes, despite the sector's current unprofitability — but present scale is not the growth trajectory the buildout is priced for.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: A 'flat but viable' AI demand outcome is bearish for anyone underwriting compounding token growth; distinguish steady-state from growth-rate exposure.
insights.quote: This may sustain the industry at something like its present scale once the infrastructure buildout is complete, despite its current unprofitability.
insights.locator: hundreds of millions of people now route their questions

insights.claim: The autonomous-agent thesis — every firm running agents that consume tokens by the billions — is inconsistent with what enterprises actually use AI for today: customer-service agents, automated Excel spreadsheets, and low-level software engineering.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: The gap between current enterprise use cases and agentic token projections is where AI capex assumptions are most likely to break.
insights.quote: the claim that every firm will see autonomous agents that consume tokens by the billions sits uneasily with these prevailing uses
insights.locator: Firms are increasingly using customer-service agents

insights.claim: If firms and consumers end up with more compute than they can name problems for, the binding constraint on growth shifts from producing goods to producing ideas — a far harder problem with no known scaling law.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: Idea supply is the unmodeled input in every AI capex forecast; treat 'what will use these tokens' as the real diligence question.
insights.quote: it will indicate a bottleneck not in the production of goods but in the production of ideas—a much harder problem to solve
insights.locator: The current buildout is a wager that there is more to come

insights.claim: Post-scarcity as an endpoint is pessimistic rather than utopian, because it describes a humanity that lacks the imagination or ambition to want anything beyond satisfying material needs.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: Inverts the standard tech-optimist narrative: the abundance thesis is itself a symptom of the demand exhaustion that stalls growth.
insights.quote: A world in which humanity lacks the imagination or ambition to strive for anything even greater than what is implied by the idea of “post-scarcity” is, upon closer inspection, a pessimistic prospect.
insights.locator: The current buildout is a wager that there is more to come

themes.theme: Gaming's Exhausted Demand Curve as Precedent

insights.claim: Video games, not administration, drove the exciting advances in computing for decades — from 1970s-80s blitters offloading repetitive graphics work, to 1990s dedicated polygon hardware, to early-2000s shader processors that justified general-purpose bulk computation.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: Consumer entertainment, not enterprise IT, has historically been the demand engine that funded compute architecture — a lesson for where the next architecture gets funded.
insights.quote: Exciting advances in computing were for a long time downstream of those working to improve the graphics of video games, not administration.
insights.locator: The Start of the Curve

insights.claim: NVIDIA's 1999 GeForce 256 was marketed as the world's first GPU for video games, and within a few years the same gaming accelerators were repurposed across science and engineering, making protein-folding simulations at least twenty times faster.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: Historical proof that general-purpose consumer hardware finds unanticipated high-value markets — the template for the CUDA-to-AI transition.
insights.quote: Protein-folding simulations became at least twenty times faster thanks to general-purpose gaming technology.
insights.locator: In 1999, NVIDIA released the GeForce 256

insights.claim: Photorealistic graphics stopped being a compute problem and became a labor-cost problem: ray tracing is now achievable on consumer hardware, and the binding constraint is paying small armies of artists, which is getting prohibitively expensive for no obviously greater spectacle.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: AAA game studios' cost structure — not GPU capability — is the ceiling on graphics; a warning that content economics, not silicon, gates a market.
insights.quote: the difficulty of photorealism in video game graphics is more a matter of game studios being able to pay small armies of artists to create realistic-looking art for the games
insights.locator: In recent years, the holy grail of photorealistic video game graphics

insights.claim: The indie game industry's twenty-year growth on stylized art that is cheaper both to produce and to render demonstrates that markets can move decisively away from compute-intensive content when the cost curve turns.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: Demand can migrate down the compute-intensity curve — a real risk pattern for anyone assuming AI usage only scales up.
insights.quote: the past twenty years have seen the growth of the indie game industry, which often uses more stylized art that is vastly cheaper, both for artists to produce and for computers to display
insights.locator: In recent years, the holy grail of photorealistic video game graphics

insights.claim: Video gaming has no obvious remaining opportunity to push computing demand: higher resolutions and more complex geometry are possible but demand does not exist at a scale that justifies them, and art costs are not sustainable as-is.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: Gaming is a structurally mature end market for GPU vendors — the AI datacenter is now the sole growth vector, concentrating risk.
insights.quote: there is no obvious remaining opportunity for video games to push computing demand
insights.locator: Because of this, there is no obvious remaining opportunity

insights.claim: Machine learning was first explored in the 1980s and only revived when GPUs caught up, illustrating a general pattern in which shelved technologies reemerge from hardware overhang — but only when some other breakthrough makes them worthwhile.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: Hardware overhang alone does not create markets; screen 'compute is finally cheap enough' pitches for the missing second breakthrough.
insights.quote: Machine learning will not be the last discarded or forgotten technology to be revived by hardware that finally caught up with it—but such technologies only ever reemerge if other breakthroughs make them worthwhile.
insights.locator: The technology that fueled the graphical development of gaming

themes.theme: Fab Cost Escalation and Competitor Extinction

insights.claim: Leading-edge fab capex has moved from a few billion dollars ten years ago to campuses now being pushed into the hundreds of billions, an order-of-magnitude escalation within a single decade.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: Capex intensity per node is the clearest quantitative measure of when the industry hits an affordability wall.
insights.quote: Ten years ago, a fabrication plant for microchips may have cost a few billion dollars to build. Today, modern fab campuses are getting pushed into the hundreds of billions.
insights.locator: Moore’s Law from the Inside

insights.claim: Photomask costs have escalated roughly 40x in three node generations — $1 million at 28nm, $10 million at 7nm, $40 million at 3nm — pushing chip tapeouts out of reach for startups that could plausibly raise $1 million but not $40 million.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: Hard numbers on why semiconductor design innovation is consolidating; venture-scale chip design at the leading edge is effectively dead.
insights.quote: from $1 million for 28-nanometer chips, to $10 million for 7 nm, to $40 million for 3 nm
insights.locator: The masks used in the photolithography processes

insights.claim: The leading-edge foundry field has collapsed from dozens of companies to just TSMC and Samsung, with Intel having fallen behind a few years ago and now receiving heavy U.S. government subsidies in hopes it can catch back up.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: Extreme supply concentration in leading-edge logic makes the AI buildout a two-supplier dependency and a state-subsidy story.
insights.quote: today, the leading chip fabs include only TSMC and Samsung, with Intel having fallen behind a few years ago and receiving heavy subsidies from the U.S. government
insights.locator: While there used to be dozens of companies at the bleeding edge

insights.claim: Semiconductor survivorship is best modeled as repeated rounds of industrial Russian roulette rather than sustained competence: companies that bet wrong on a manufacturing process transition are permanently removed from the cutting edge.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: Treat incumbent leading-edge foundries as path-dependent survivors, not durable moats — one bad node bet is terminal.
insights.quote: those that have survived the decades are to a large extent merely those who have survived the most rounds of industrial Russian roulette as manufacturing processes changed
insights.locator: In the semiconductor space, it is common for companies that bet wrong

insights.claim: AMD founder Jerry Sanders' famous 'real men own fabs' critique of the fabless model was empirically defeated: five years after he stepped down as chairman, AMD spun its fabs into GlobalFoundries, which then declared it would stop competing on the most advanced manufacturing processes.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: Case study in how exponential operating costs force vertical disintegration — the same logic now pressuring anyone contemplating owning AI silicon end-to-end.
insights.quote: real men own fabs
insights.locator: Jerry Sanders, founder of AMD, famously used to claim

insights.claim: TSMC pioneered the open-foundry model only in 1987, nineteen years after Intel's founding, and before that it was common for small chip startups in the 1970s and 1980s to own their own fabs — a reminder that today's structure is recent and contingent.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: Industry structure has flipped once already within living memory; assume it can flip again under cost pressure.
insights.quote: TSMC, an early pioneer in this business model, was not founded until 1987, a whole nineteen years after the founding of Intel.
insights.locator: Moore’s Law from the Inside

insights.claim: Foundries like TSMC may eventually be forced to charge prices that few if any of their fabless customers can afford, breaking the customer base that funds each successive node.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: Watch foundry wafer pricing versus fabless gross margins as the early warning that node progression is becoming uneconomic.
insights.quote: foundries like TSMC may eventually be forced to charge prices that few if any of their fabless customers can afford
insights.locator: Raising $1 million for a 28 nm chip tapeout

insights.claim: Pushing semiconductor technology further may eventually exceed what even the most deep-pocketed nation-states can pay, making the cost curve a geopolitical rather than corporate ceiling.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: Reframes chip sovereignty programs as potentially unaffordable for everyone, not just for laggards — a long-dated tail risk to the entire compute thesis.
insights.quote: it is a serious possibility that pushing semiconductor technology further may exceed what even the most deep-pocketed nation-states are capable of paying
insights.locator: With fabs being as expensive as they are

insights.claim: AI companies are very good at raising large sums on product hype while their actual profitability is questionable, with some industry leaders accusing them of overcharging — and LLMs alone are unlikely to justify a trillion-dollar superfab.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: The financing chain from AI revenue to next-generation fab capex has an unproven middle link; this is where the cycle would break.
insights.quote: it’s not clear that LLMs alone will be nearly sufficient to justify building a trillion-dollar superfab
insights.locator: AI companies are currently very good at raising large sums

insights.claim: Extrapolating a decade forward from exponentially rising fab costs and exponentially falling competitor counts yields fab costs in the trillions of dollars and approximately zero companies able to keep up.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: A quantifiable end-date framing for leading-edge scaling that investors can test against actual node cost disclosures.
insights.quote: Extrapolating these trends another decade suggests fab costs in the trillions of dollars and approximately zero companies that can keep up.
insights.locator: The cost of building a competitive semiconductor fab has grown exponentially

themes.theme: Idea Veins and Diminishing Returns to Scaling

insights.claim: Ideas come in veins like minerals: a sufficiently general idea can be applied across an in-principle infinite range of similarly shaped problems, most simply through arbitrary scaling — throwing more resources at the same formula to solve bigger instances of the same kind.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: A mental model for judging whether a technology has real optionality or only linear scale-up left; the latter is where returns die.
insights.quote: ideas, like minerals, come in veins
insights.locator: Branching Veins

insights.claim: LLM inference — the 'thinking' that goes into generating an answer — now exceeds training in compute cost, the clearest instance of arbitrary scaling absorbing hardware.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: Inference-dominant compute mix changes the hardware, memory, and power profile of the buildout versus a training-led one.
insights.quote: When it comes to LLMs, this is why inference—the “thinking” that goes into the generation of an answer—now exceeds training in terms of compute costs.
insights.locator: Branching Veins

insights.claim: Scalable ideas hit two hard limits — the value of larger problems may diminish, or the cost of solving them may rise too fast — exactly as with mineral and oil deposits that go untapped because concentration is too low or extraction too expensive relative to easier sources.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: The resource-extraction analogy gives a concrete test for AI scaling: compare marginal value of the next capability tier against its marginal cost.
insights.quote: There is no shortage of deposits throughout the world containing valuable minerals that are too low in concentration or too difficult to extract at reasonable prices with existing technology.
insights.locator: This may also support scaling in multiple different dimensions

insights.claim: Even with scaling laws providing a clear roadmap, their exponential nature may outrun fab technology so that compute requirements and costs grow faster than revenue, making the roadmap unfundable rather than impossible.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: The bear case for AI is a financing failure, not a technical one — track cost-per-capability against revenue-per-capability.
insights.quote: The compute requirements, and by extension the costs, may grow faster than revenue.
insights.locator: Even though scaling laws provide a clear roadmap

insights.claim: If human imagination and ambition yield diminishing returns past a certain quantity of compute, the resulting applications will be insufficient to fund the development of greater compute, creating a self-terminating loop.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: Names the feedback mechanism by which a demand shortfall becomes a permanent halt in supply-side progress, not a pause.
insights.quote: if our imagination and ambition yield diminishing returns past a certain quantity of compute, these applications may be insufficient to fund the development of greater compute
insights.locator: There are many problems we can apply computation to

insights.claim: Rephrasing 'post-scarcity' as 'overproduction' reveals it as an old problem already addressed by thinkers from John Stuart Mill to Toyota's Taiichi Ohno, who held overproduction to be a worse problem than underproduction because it reflects inefficiencies in the demand-production pipeline.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: Applies lean-manufacturing waste theory to AI datacenter capex — a rare, testable analytical lens on the buildout.
insights.quote: recognized overproduction as a greater problem than underproduction, because it reflects inefficiencies in the demand-production pipeline that lead to compounding waste through overprocessing, transport, waiting, and defects
insights.locator: If we simply rephrase “post-scarcity” as “overproduction,”

insights.claim: AI scaling laws invert Taiichi Ohno's demand-pull principle — modeled on the American supermarket shelf restocked only as customers empty it — because compute yields more capability without any evidence the capability will find a buyer.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: The industry's core planning doctrine is push-production in a discipline that learned decades ago that push production destroys value.
insights.quote: Compute yields more capability, yes, but that says nothing about whether the capability will find a buyer. The trillion-dollar fab is production running far ahead of any order.
insights.locator: Ohno’s preference was to let demand pull production

insights.claim: The post-scarcity thesis is fallacious because human needs could already have been declared satisfied after the twentieth century's agricultural revolutions or the spread of cars and air-conditioning; beyond that point technology only develops to serve desires that exceed needs.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: Implies the growth rate of technology is a function of cultural ambition, an input no capex model contains.
insights.quote: After a certain point, technology develops only to account for desires beyond human needs. The future will be brought into existence only by people with a concrete desire to outstrip those needs.
insights.locator: Moore’s Law can and will grind to a halt

insights.claim: Moore's Law can and will grind to a halt if human innovation cannot find applications for the vast compute already produced, making stagnation a demand-side outcome rather than a physics limit.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: The central call: bet on application-layer imagination as the leading indicator for the entire semiconductor complex.
insights.quote: Moore’s Law can and will grind to a halt if human innovation cannot find applications for the vast amount of compute we have produced.
insights.locator: Moore’s Law can and will grind to a halt

insights.claim: Semiconductor advancement may slow purely from a lack of profitable scalability that is downstream of industrial society's aggregate demand, even where further advancement remains theoretically possible.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: Links chip-cycle forecasting to macro aggregate demand rather than to engineering roadmaps.
insights.quote: advances in semiconductors may simply slow down in response to a lack of profitable scalability, which is downstream of industrial society’s aggregate demand. This is a recipe for stagnation.
insights.locator: The cost of building a competitive semiconductor fab has grown exponentially

themes.theme: The Primitive-Adoption Test for Real Technology

insights.claim: The test separating useful from overbuilt technology is that useful technology sees widespread adoption even while primitive — if the benefits outweigh the costs, people adopt it regardless of its drawbacks.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: A fast screen for hype categories: check whether the crude early version already found organic users before the polish arrived.
insights.quote: What separates useful from overbuilt technology is that the former sees widespread adoption even while primitive.
insights.locator: What separates useful from overbuilt technology

insights.claim: Virtual reality fails the primitive-adoption test: had it been seriously useful it would have gained wide adoption during the metaverse boom, and the insistence that it must first be made far more convenient is itself evidence of a lack of genuine value.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: Explicit worked example of production exceeding usefulness — apply the same test to current AI hardware categories.
insights.quote: if the technology must be made much more convenient before significant adoption can occur, as so many insist, the effort to diminish its inconveniences suggests a lack of genuine value to begin with
insights.locator: What separates useful from overbuilt technology

insights.claim: VR is characterized as production exceeding our current ability to find meaningful use, with the caveat that this may change in coming decades as deeper thought is applied to its design problems — the failure is conceptual, not technological.
insights.speaker: Charles Rosenbauer
insights.so_what: Distinguishes 'dead' from 'awaiting an idea' — the same distinction that determines whether AI hardware overhang eventually pays off.
insights.quote: VR is an example of production exceeding our current ability to find a meaningful use for a technology, and this may change in coming decades as deeper thought is applied to the various design problems around virtual reality.
insights.locator: What separates useful from overbuilt technology
